name: assertion-builder
intent: Issue a signed authentication, identity or delegation assertion from one controlled component: assemble the issuer's canonical claim profile, apply protected signing-key material, and publish the matching verification key so a relying party can validate a statement about a subject without sharing a session or reproducing issuance policy.
problem: Different trust domains need a portable statement - this user authenticated, this service may act for that tenant, this client is authorised - but a relying party must not accept an arbitrary claim set just because it is well formed. The issuer therefore needs one policy-driven component that fixes the subject, issuer, audience, validity window and replay identifier, signs the exact SAML or JWT representation, and makes the corresponding verification material discoverable without putting private-key handling in every call site.
context: Identity providers and security-token services that hand assertions to parties outside their own process: an IdP returning a SAML Response containing an Assertion, an OpenID Provider minting an ID Token, an OAuth 2.0 authorisation server accepting or issuing a private_key_jwt client assertion, a token-exchange service producing a new audience-restricted token, or a gateway issuing narrow delegation claims. It applies when the issuer owns a trust anchor (a signing key whose verification material is published or pre-provisioned) and consumers enforce a stable claim profile; it does not apply when a shared session store or an in-process authorisation check already answers the trust question.
benefits: One definition of what an assertion is: issuer identity, claim names, audience restriction and lifetime are set in a single component, so every token the organisation issues has the same semantics instead of one hand-built variant per call site.

Cryptographic plumbing is isolated from application logic: serialization, signing algorithm and key selection sit behind the signer, and private key material never reaches the code that decides who receives an assertion.

Key rotation and algorithm agility become configuration: a key id plus published verification material (JWKS, SAML metadata, certificates) lets consumers follow rotations without code changes on either side.

Mandatory policy is enforced once: required expiry, audience, issuer and replay id can be built into the API, so no call site can mint an eternal, audience-free bearer assertion by forgetting a field.
Testability: claim assembly is ordinary data and can be asserted directly, while a fake signer produces deterministic assertions; one real end-to-end signature test then covers the crypto path.
Format independence: keeping claim assembly separate from serialization lets the same statement be issued as a SAML assertion or a JWT when different consumers require different token formats.
tradeoffs: Minting power is concentrated: whatever can drive this component - or reach its key - can assert any identity, so the builder is high-value attack surface that needs its own review, logging and least-privilege deployment.

Integrity is not authorisation: the assertion is cryptographically sound, but consumers still own issuer, audience, expiry and replay checks, so a perfectly signed token can be accepted by the wrong party or honoured after it should have been rejected.

No revocation inside the validity window: a self-contained assertion stays valid until it expires, so revoking one requires short lifetimes plus an external store or introspection, which gives back the statelessness the format promised.

The claim schema couples issuer and consumers: renaming or retyping a claim is a coordinated release across every verifier, and drift between what the builder emits and what consumers enforce stays silent until an incident.

Configuration fragility with a binary outcome: algorithms, key ids, clock skew and TTL policy must all be right; a mistake usually fails closed and takes authentication down globally, or fails open if a fallback path signs with a weaker algorithm.

Opaque artefacts are hard to debug: assertions look like random strings until decoded and their failures surface on the consumer side, so issuance metadata (key id, expiry, replay id) must travel with the token to make incidents traceable.

participants.responsibility: Supplies the semantics: subject identity, attributes or roles, intended audience and intended lifetime, taken from an authentication result, a directory or a policy decision; knows nothing about serialization or cryptography and cannot choose the signing key.

Assembles the canonical profile (issuer, subject, audience, validity window and replay identifier), applies protocol-specific requirements such as SAML SubjectConfirmation or OIDC nonce-related claims, asks the signing authority to protect the exact serialized bytes, and returns the assertion with issuance metadata (key id, expiry and replay id).

Holds or reaches the issuer's private key (keystore, HSM or KMS) and applies the profile's agreed algorithm; key material never leaves this role, and the builder addresses a key id or key handle rather than a raw secret.

Keeps verification material current and reachable - SAML metadata or an X.509 certificate, or a JWKS endpoint keyed by kid - publishes the new key before a rotation cutover, and retires old keys only after all assertions they signed can no longer be accepted.

The relying party that validates the signature and protocol conditions before trusting any claim: issuer, audience, expiry, replay id and, where applicable, SAML Destination/InResponseTo or OIDC nonce and azp; it then maps the claims onto a local principal.

use_cases: An identity provider such as a Keycloak realm issuing SAML authentication or attribute assertions for registered service providers, which validate the response against the IdP's published metadata and audience restrictions.
An OpenID Provider such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta minting ID Tokens for a registered client, with issuer, client audience, nonce-related checks and short expiration enforced by the relying party.

A Spring Security/OpenSAML service provider receiving a signed SAML Response at its assertion consumer service, where the provider validates the response issuer, destination, assertion signatures, time conditions and audience before creating a local principal.

An OAuth 2.0 authorisation server issuing access tokens or accepting a short-lived private_key_jwt client assertion, with the verifier selecting the registered public key by kid and pinning the permitted algorithm.

An API gateway or sidecar issuing narrow delegation tokens that carry the original subject and scope for downstream services, which verify them against the gateway's public keys rather than trusting the upstream token blindly.
Distributed approval workflows: a decision taken in one service travels as a signed statement (who approved what, for which audience, until when) to services that never share a session.
Integration and contract tests that mint valid assertions - including deliberately expired, wrong-audience and replayed cases - without weakening the production issuer.

SAML-to-JWT token translation at an API Gateway: the gateway acts as a SAML SP, translates the SAML assertion into a short-lived JWT (for example, a 15-minute TTL), and filters claims to the minimum required by downstream services, preventing PII sprawl across microservices.

OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693): a Security Token Service exchanges an upstream assertion (SAML, JWT or refresh token) for a new, narrowly scoped assertion targeting a specific resource server, supporting delegation and impersonation semantics through act and may_act claims.

Multi-domain federation with typed JWTs: an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG, per IETF draft) chains an upstream OIDC ID Token or SAML assertion across trust domains without re-prompting the user, using a distinct typ value to prevent cross-JWT confusion.
avoid_when: The credential never leaves your own system and revocation must be immediate: use a Secure Session Manager with an opaque, server-side session id rather than a self-contained bearer assertion.

A managed identity provider or cloud security-token service already issues the assertions: federate with it and configure the claim profile instead of operating a second issuer and key-rotation pipeline.

You only need confidentiality between your own tiers, not a portable statement another trust domain must verify: use authenticated encryption, a server-controlled cookie or a database lookup instead of a signing authority.
The assertion is a fixed test fixture: use a checked-in fixture or a test-only signer rather than standing up production issuance policy to produce one constant token.

You cannot hold a signing key safely yet (no KMS/HSM, secrets copied into every replica): fix key custody first, because an assertion builder without protected keys multiplies exposure instead of reducing it.

A local authorisation decision is enough and no downstream component needs a portable proof: call the Authorisation Enforcer at the boundary instead of serialising a claim that another component may misinterpret.
anti_patterns: "String concatenation as JOSE": gluing base64 segments together or writing XML signatures without a tested library, so padding, encoding and canonicalisation bugs produce assertions that verify nowhere - or, worse, verify too broadly.
Trusting the algorithm from the assertion: letting the token header pick alg, or leaving an unsigned alg=none path reachable, which is the classic algorithm-confusion hole (CWE-327, OWASP A02:2021).
Eternal, audience-free bearer assertions with no exp, no aud and no jti, so a single leaked token is valid forever and everywhere.
One component that issues and validates with the same key material, blurring the trust boundary and usually weakening validation until the happy path passes.
Claims as a database dump: shipping the whole user record, internal identifiers or personal data inside an assertion that then travels to every consumer and log sink.
A builder that also decides authorisation - granting privileges rather than stating them - turning the issuer into an accidental policy engine.
JWKS fetching from unvalidated URLs in the token header: trusting jku, x5u or jwk from the assertion enables key-injection forgery; the verification key must be anchored out-of-band.
SAML assertion replay without ID tracking: issuing assertions with predictable IDs and not checking for replay allows captured assertions to be replayed within their validity window.
HMAC secrets shared across audiences: using the same symmetric key for HS256 with multiple audiences allows one audience to forge tokens for another (OWASP JWT Cheat Sheet).
Stateful session cookies in stateless APIs: replicating the browser cookie session model for microservices breaks statelessness and complicates horizontal scaling.

SAML signature wrapping: verifying one signed Assertion but consuming a second attacker-controlled Assertion lets forged claims win; bind the signature reference to the exact node whose claims are mapped.

Cross-token substitution: accepting an ID Token where an access token or client assertion is expected confuses token purpose and audience; require a distinct typ/profile and mutually exclusive validation rules.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: claim assembly, cryptographic protection and key publication are three responsibilities with different failure modes.
Single source of truth for identity: the issuer name and its keys are configured once and reused, never re-derived per call site.
Dependency inversion: the builder depends on a signer abstraction, so algorithms and key backends (file keystore, HSM, KMS) are swappable without touching claim logic.
Information hiding and least privilege: only the signing authority sees private key material, and only for the algorithm it is configured to use.
Fail-safe defaults: expiry, audience and an explicit algorithm are mandatory, so a missing policy denies issuance instead of minting a broadly valid assertion.
Cryptographic agility: algorithms and key types are configuration, not code; the builder must support algorithm switching without a deployment.
Explicit typing for JWTs: use the typ header (e.g., application/oauth-id-jag+jwt) to prevent cross-JWT confusion when the same issuer emits multiple token types.
Algorithm pinning at the verifier: never trust the token's alg header; always validate against an explicitly configured allowlist.
Type-safe keys: pass typed key objects (not raw strings or byte arrays) to verification functions to prevent HMAC vs RSA key-type confusion attacks.
Minimal claim disclosure: issue only the claims each consumer needs; filter at the gateway rather than passing raw upstream assertions to all downstream services.
best_practices: Make profile-required fields mandatory in the builder API: SAML Issuer, ID, IssueInstant, Conditions and SubjectConfirmation, or JWT iss, aud, iat and exp plus jti when replay detection is required.
Sign with asymmetric algorithms (RS256/PS256/ES256) for anything crossing a trust boundary, and keep shared-secret HS256 for tokens that never leave one system.
Keep the private key in a KMS/HSM or keystore and sign by key reference; publish only public material, and rotate with overlapping validity by publishing the new key before signing with it.
Pin the algorithm per key on the consumer side, reject alg=none outright and treat the alg header as untrusted input.
Keep assertions short-lived and audience-restricted, and pair jti with a replay store whenever the same assertion could be presented twice.
Return issuance metadata with the token (key id, expiry, replay id, claim-profile version) and audit issuance - issuer, subject, audience, key id - without logging the assertion itself.
Version the claim profile and test it as a contract: decode-and-assert the expected claims in each consumer, plus one test that verifies a real signature end to end.
Use ECDSA deterministic signatures (RFC 6979) to prevent private-key recovery from predictable nonces; verify r and s are non-zero to block CVE-2022-21449.

For SAML assertions: preserve the signed XML tree, use the profile's required canonicalisation method, and let the library place the Signature element according to the SAML schema instead of hand-editing the DOM after signing.

For large SAML responses, use a hardened streaming or bounded XML parser where the library supports it, but keep signature-reference binding and entity-expansion protections enabled; measure memory rather than assuming a fixed reduction.
For typed JWTs, include the typ header per RFC 8725 §3.11; validation rules for different token types must be mutually exclusive (different alg, aud, or key per type).
Implement certificate-expiry monitoring with alerts at 30, 14, and 7 days before expiration; use automated renewal to prevent outages.
Rate-limit token exchange endpoints (e.g., 100 requests/minute per IP) to limit token-forgery brute-force and denial-of-service attacks.
For API Gateway translation: issue short-lived JWTs (≤15 minutes) from SAML assertions and filter claims to the minimum required per downstream service, preventing PII sprawl.
Test the full issuance flow (claim assembly → sign → serialize → decode → verify) with both valid and invalid inputs; test replay detection separately.

related_patterns_notes.authenticator: establishes a local identity from credentials; Assertion Builder packages an already-authenticated subject into a portable statement for another trust domain.
related_patterns_notes.subject-descriptor: describes a subject's identity data; Assertion Builder signs a bounded claim profile so a consumer can verify who made the statement.
related_patterns_notes.security-context: carries the current principal inside one process or request; Assertion Builder creates a portable assertion that can cross that boundary.
related_patterns_notes.secure-session-manager: keeps a revocable server-side session handle; Assertion Builder issues a self-contained assertion whose lifetime and replay policy must be enforced by consumers.
related_patterns_notes.authorization-enforcer: evaluates a request against local policy; Assertion Builder only states signed claims and must not grant privileges by itself.
related_patterns_notes.audit-interceptor: records an accountability event; Assertion Builder creates a credential or delegation statement that a consumer may later audit.
related_patterns_notes.reference-monitor: mediates every local access to a protected resource; Assertion Builder supplies signed evidence to a remote verifier and cannot replace local mediation.
related_patterns_notes.federated-identity: defines the trust and identifier lifecycle between organisations; Assertion Builder materialises one assertion within that federation.
related_patterns_notes.security-token-service-sts: exchanges or validates credentials at a token boundary; Assertion Builder is the issuer-side component that produces the new profile.
related_patterns_notes.api-gateway-identity-translator: maps an inbound identity to a downstream representation at the gateway; Assertion Builder is the narrower claim-and-signing responsibility used to produce that representation.
related_patterns_notes.token-exchange: transforms one subject token into another token for a target resource; Assertion Builder supplies the controlled issuance step but does not define exchange authorisation.
related_patterns_notes.claim-based-access-control: makes an access decision from claims; Assertion Builder supplies signed claims while leaving policy evaluation to the consumer.
